comparison: Both evaluate dataset quality and experimental design (C6, C27, C39-C44). OpenEval provides detailed technical validation of library depth and gene detection. Peer reviewers praise the dataset as 'exceptional' and 'high quality,' confirming the same claims. Peer R1 also includes clustering claims (C45-C47) not in OpenEval R1.

OpenEval R2 addresses clustering and cell type identification (C45-C48). Peer R1 includes these claims (C45-C47) as part of broader dataset validation, praising the comprehensive coverage. Both support the clustering approach, though peer review groups this with overall data quality rather than as separate evaluation.

OpenEval R3 evaluates absence of mature neuronal markers (C49-C51) as biologically plausible for the developmental timeframe. Peer R17 accepts these as supporting observations that provide biological context, without detailed discussion but no disagreement.

Both address temporal analysis and DC0 correlation with developmental stage (C52-C57). OpenEval emphasizes validation through cadherin switch. Peer R2 confirms successful temporal mapping, with reviewers noting the study produces 'highly detailed temporal map' and successfully 'infer temporal gene expression dynamics.'

OpenEval R5 validates DC0 temporal ordering through E-cadherin to N-cadherin switch (C58-C64). Peer R2 encompasses temporal analysis broadly (C58-C62 included) and confirms the temporal characterization is successful. Both support multi-level validation approach.

OpenEval R6 describes temporal gene expression changes (C65-C67). Peer R10 accepts these findings as part of comprehensive temporal characterization, noting data revealed 'known and novel genes' along developmental axes. Both support the biological interpretation.

Both evaluate region-specific gene expression patterns (C68-C77). OpenEval provides detailed validation of specific markers. Peer R10 confirms these findings are central to the study's contribution, with editor noting 'known and novel genes differentially expressed along rostro-caudal...axes.'

OpenEval R8 validates spatial ordering analysis (C78-C84) against known markers. Peer R3 strongly validates the computational approach, with Reviewer 2 stating 'validation...using published gene expression patterns is convincing' and noting 'good agreement.' Both emphasize the 87% validation rate.

OpenEval R9 addresses anterior-posterior patterned gene identification (C85-C86, C89). Peer R3 validates this as part of the comprehensive spatial analysis, praising it as 'well-validated against sets of genes with known temporal and spatial patterns.' Both support the modular organization conclusion.

Both evaluate validation of spatial predictions (C90-C93). OpenEval notes 87% agreement rate and reasonable explanation for discrepancies. Peer R3 confirms validation is 'convincing' with 'good agreement,' supporting the predictive capability of the approach.

Both address spatially patterned transcription factors (C94-C97). OpenEval validates specific genes as established regulators. Peer R6 explicitly praises 'emphasis on transcription factors' providing 'valuable insights into...gene regulatory networks,' confirming functional context.

Both evaluate mediolateral spatial analysis (C101-C106). OpenEval validates DC2 correlation with known markers. Peer R4 accepts mediolateral patterning as part of comprehensive spatial characterization, with reviewers noting findings along 'medio-lateral axes.' Both support the approach.

OpenEval R13 validates mediolateral predictions with 86% agreement (C107-C108). Peer R4 accepts this as consistent with anterior-posterior validation, supporting the reliability of spatial prediction approach across both axes.

Both address mediolaterally patterned transcription factors (C109-C111). OpenEval validates genes as established regulators with functional annotations. Peer R11 accepts these as part of mediolateral analysis revealing 'characteristic changes in gene expression along the mediolateral axis.'

OpenEval R15 describes overlap between anterior-posterior and mediolateral patterning (C113-C115). Peer R17 accepts these as supporting observations strengthening main findings, without detailed discussion but no disagreement on the integration of patterning systems.

Both evaluate multiscale spatial analysis (C116-C119). OpenEval describes identification of 870 genes reflecting combined spatial inputs. Peer R5 acknowledges multidimensional analysis as key contribution, with reviewers praising comprehensive characterization along both axes.

Both address multiscale clustering approach (C120-C125). OpenEval demonstrates ability to distinguish patterns at different resolutions. Peer R5 praises the multidimensional spatial analysis strategy, confirming it provides effective characterization at multiple scales.

Perfect claim overlap (C126-C131). Both evaluate comparison between cranial and spinal cord patterning. OpenEval provides detailed analysis of two-dimensional patterning complexity. Peer R9 accepts this as part of comprehensive characterization, though not extensively discussed by reviewers.

Both address spatially patterned signaling molecules (C136-C138). OpenEval validates identification of known pathways and neural tube closure genes. Peer R12 confirms these findings validate the spatial analysis approach and notes resource will be valuable for examining 'signaling molecules...controlling regionalization.'

Both evaluate SAG treatment experimental design (C145-C151). OpenEval validates experimental design, phenotypic observations, and dataset quality. Peer R7 accepts the SHH signaling analysis, with Reviewer 2 describing the transcriptome analysis revealing 'characteristic changes' and 'distinct Shh regulated gene expression programs.'

High claim overlap (C152-C156). Both evaluate changes in known SHH pathway components. OpenEval validates upregulation of positive targets and downregulation of negative regulators. Peer R13 accepts these as demonstrating successful SHH pathway activation, serving as positive controls.

Both address connection between SAG treatment and spatial analysis (C157-C161). OpenEval quantifies overlap and interprets region-specific responses. Peer R7 confirms the analysis revealed 'distinct Shh regulated gene expression programs in the developing fore-, mid- and hindbrain,' supporting integration of patterning systems.

Perfect claim overlap (C162-C166). Both evaluate region-specific SAG responses. OpenEval provides specific examples supporting integration of patterning systems. Peer R14 directly supports these findings, with Reviewer 2 explicitly noting 'distinct Shh regulated gene expression programs' in different brain regions.

Both provide integrative interpretation of SAG and spatial analysis (C167-C168). OpenEval concludes cross-regulation between patterning systems based on region-specific responses. Peer R7 accepts this interpretation as part of the comprehensive SHH signaling analysis that reviewers found convincing.

High claim overlap on WNT pathway effects (C169-C175). OpenEval describes downregulation of WNT components and interprets antagonism with SHH. Peer R8 acknowledges cross-pathway interactions, with Reviewer 1 specifically mentioning 'including the Wnt pathway' among findings, though mechanistic interpretation noted as speculative.

Both address downregulation of neuronal function genes with disease associations (C176). OpenEval notes consistency with pre-neurogenic state. Peer R15 accepts this as part of comprehensive SAG analysis, noting resource will be valuable for understanding 'pathological signaling outcomes,' though connection is speculative.

Both summarize validation results (C185-C186). OpenEval cites 87% and 86% validation rates for anterior-posterior and mediolateral analyses. Peer R3 strongly validates the approach, with reviewers stating validation is 'convincing' and approach is 'well-validated,' supporting predictive capability.

Both address summary claims about spatial gene identification (C7-C8, C32-C34). OpenEval connects to detailed validation results. Peer R3 confirms the computational approach successfully identified genes along both axes, with editor noting 'known and novel genes differentially expressed.'

Both evaluate summary claims about SAG experiment (C9-C10, C37-C38). OpenEval emphasizes distinct regional programs and interplay between patterning systems. Peer R7 confirms these findings, with reviewers noting 'distinct Shh regulated gene expression programs' in different brain regions.

Peer R6 emphasizes the value of identifying transcription factors, cell surface, and secreted proteins (C94, C109, C136) for understanding gene regulatory networks. While OpenEval R11, R14, and R19 address these claims individually, Peer R6 uniquely highlights the collective emphasis on these molecule types as a key contribution.

Peer R16 validates extensive background claims and knowledge gaps (C1-C5, C11-C26, C28, C95-C100, C132-C144, C146, C171, C188-C189) that frame the study's motivation. OpenEval does not separately evaluate these foundational/background claims, focusing instead on the study's novel findings and analyses.
